title: Pressure Now, Justice When He Comes
sum: The letter opens with the same three names as 1 Thessalonians: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, writing to a young church in the Macedonian capital (1:1-2). Paul gives thanks that the believers' faith and love are growing even as persecution goes on, and says he boasts of them to other churches (1:3-4).

Then, in one long Greek sentence (1:3-10), he sets their suffering inside God's justice. Their endurance is a sign that God's verdict will be right: those who press hard on them will be pressed in turn, and they will be given rest when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels, in a flame of fire. The picture borrows the words of Isaiah 2 and 66, where the LORD comes to judge, and gives that role to Jesus. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will make them fit for his calling, so that Jesus' name is honored in them (1:11-12).
readings: Read as comfort for the persecuted

The first hearers were a small, pressured group of converts. What they needed was assurance that their suffering was not a sign of God's displeasure, and that the people harming them would not have the last word. Read this way, 1:5-10 is not a cool doctrine of hell but a promise of justice, given to people who were not allowed to defend themselves and were told not to repay evil for evil (1 Thessalonians 5:15).
Read as a teaching on the last judgment

Church teaching has long taken 1:7-10 as one of the clearest New Testament statements of the final judgment: Christ's return in glory, the punishment of those who reject the gospel, and the glory of the saints. The Westminster Confession quotes these verses in its chapter on the Last Judgment (33.2). Here the questions are what 'eternal ruin' means and who exactly is judged; the notes and the card give the answers.
Read as a Jewish apocalyptic scene

The chapter is built from the Scriptures of Israel: the LORD coming in fire (Isaiah 66:15), people fleeing from his face and the glory of his strength (Isaiah 2:10, 19, 21), God glorified among his holy ones (Psalm 89:7), and the punishment of nations that do not know him (Jeremiah 10:25). Like Daniel 7 and 12, it promises the persecuted faithful that God will vindicate them. The new element is that the coming one is the Lord Jesus.

views.H: Thessalonica was the chief city of Roman Macedonia. Acts 17:1-9 shows the church born in conflict: a riot, Jason's house stormed, and the charge that the believers said "that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7). 1 Thessalonians 2:14 says the converts suffered from their own countrymen. If Paul wrote soon after 1 Thessalonians, the letter comes from Corinth in about AD 51-52, while Silas and Timothy were with him (Acts 18:5); the persecution was still going on ("you are bearing", 1:4). Gentile converts who stopped honoring their city's and families' gods could lose friends, trade and standing, and could be suspected of disloyalty.
views.C: Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the letter point to chapter 1 first. The thanksgiving repeats the shape and words of 1 Thessalonians 1:2-3, and twice uses "we are obliged to give thanks" (1:3; 2:13), which some hear as stiff beside the warmth of 1 Thessalonians. The judgment scene is long and vivid, unlike anything in 1 Thessalonians. On this view the letter was written about AD 80-115 (Menken). Defenders of Paul answer that the repetition fits a second letter written weeks later to the same people about the same crisis, and that the judgment scene answers a new need: persecution had grown (Malherbe, Wanamaker).
views.L: In the Greek, 1:3-10 is a single sentence that begins as a thanksgiving and turns into a vision of judgment. It is built on a reversal: those who "trouble" will receive "trouble" (1:6), the troubled will receive "rest" (1:7). It ends on the words "on that day", which lead into chapter 2's question about the day. A prayer (1:11-12) rounds off the chapter, as Paul's thanksgivings often do. Words of glory frame the whole: Christ glorified in his saints (1:10), his name glorified in them (1:12).
views.J: Almost every phrase of 1:7-10 comes from the Greek Old Testament: "in a flame of fire" and "paying back" from Isaiah 66:15; "from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his strength" from Isaiah 2:10, 19, 21; "those who do not know God" from Jeremiah 10:25 and Psalm 79:6; "glorified in his saints" from Psalm 89:7. In those texts the one who comes is the LORD, Israel's God. Here he is "the Lord Jesus". A Jewish reader would see a very high claim for Jesus, and would also recognize the hope of Daniel 7 and 12: the persecuted faithful vindicated at God's judgment.
views.T: The chapter shaped Christian teaching on the last judgment. The Westminster Confession (33.2) cites 1:7-10 for the wicked being "punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord". The meaning of "eternal ruin" (1:9) divides the churches today: see the card.

deep.b:
Modern readers are often uneasy with 1:6-9: God will "give back trouble" and the persecutors will "pay the penalty". Several things are worth noticing. First, the readers are not told to take revenge; the vengeance is God's, as in Deuteronomy 32:35 and Romans 12:19, and 1 Thessalonians 5:15 forbids paying back evil. Leaving judgment to God is what makes it possible not to retaliate. Second, the language is the language of a court: "just judgment", "right in God's sight", "penalty" (dike). The concern is that wrong done to the powerless will not simply be forgotten. Third, the penalty is described in the Old Testament's own words (Isaiah 2 and 66), as the judgment of the day of the LORD.

Some readers still find the passage harsh, and some critical scholars count its tone as one sign that Paul did not write it. Others note that people under persecution, then and now, have found it a comfort: the God they trust sees what is done to them. Both responses have a long history.

Put the Old Testament sources side by side with 1:7-10 and a pattern appears. In Isaiah 66:15 the LORD comes in fire; here it is "the Lord Jesus" in "a flame of fire". In Isaiah 2:10 people hide from the face of the LORD and the glory of his strength; here the punishment is "from the face of the Lord", Jesus. In Psalm 89:7 (in the Greek) God is glorified in the council of the holy ones; here Christ comes "to have his glory shown in his saints". In Zechariah 14:5 the LORD comes with all his holy ones; here the Lord Jesus comes with his angels.

Paul does not argue for this; he simply speaks of Jesus in the words the Scriptures use for God, as he does in Philippians 2:10-11 with Isaiah 45:23. Many scholars see this as one of the earliest signs of how the first Christians spoke of Jesus. Jewish readers, ancient and modern, have seen the same move and judged it differently.

echoes: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-3; 1 Thessalonians 2:14; Acts 17:1-9; Isaiah 2:10; Isaiah 2:19; Isaiah 2:21; Isaiah 66:15; Psalm 89:7; Jeremiah 10:25; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 7:9-10; Matthew 25:31-46; Romans 12:19; 1 Corinthians 1:7

settings.by: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, as the letter names them
settings.to: the church of the Thessalonians: mostly Gentile converts, with some Jews and God-fearers (Acts 17:4), in the chief city of Roman Macedonia
settings.when: if Paul wrote it, from Corinth about AD 51-52, weeks or months after 1 Thessalonians; if a follower wrote it, some decades later
settings.why: to open the letter with the authority of the three men who founded the church, and with grace and peace. The greeting is almost word for word that of 1 Thessalonians, which is why the relation between the two letters is the first question of the book.
views: The three are together in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and write again to the same church soon after the first letter (Malherbe; Wanamaker, who thinks this letter came first).
A later writer in Paul's name
A follower copied the opening of 1 Thessalonians to write to Paul's churches in a new situation, perhaps 80-115 (Menken, Trilling).

settings.what: Thanksgiving, and the promise of God's just judgment
settings.to: the believers at Thessalonica, under ongoing persecution from their neighbors
settings.when: while the persecution continues (1:4), and before the letter turns to the false claim that the day of the Lord has come (2:2)
settings.why: to tell people who were suffering for their faith that their endurance is noticed and praised, that their suffering is not a sign of God's rejection, and that God will right the wrong when the Lord Jesus comes. Knowing the readers were a small persecuted minority changes how 1:6-9 sounds: it is a promise of justice to the powerless, not a threat to outsiders.
settings.readers: Gentile converts who had given up their gods and lost standing for it would hear that the Lord they now served would be revealed openly, and that the honor they lacked now would be given to them in his presence.

settings.when: at the end of the thanksgiving, as in most of Paul's letters
settings.why: to turn the vision of the end into a present prayer: that God will make them fit for his calling and complete their good desires and works of faith now, so that Jesus' name is honored in their lives before it is honored on the last day.

traditions.q: Does 'eternal ruin' (1:9) mean endless punishment, or that the lost come to an end?
views: The Church affirms that hell exists and is eternal, and that its chief punishment is "eternal separation from God" (Catechism 1035). It also teaches that "we cannot be united with God unless we freely choose to love him" (Catechism 1033).

Endless punishment. The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow (1839) asks what the lot of unbelievers and transgressors will be, and answers: "They will be given over to everlasting death, that is, to everlasting fire, to everlasting torment, with the devils" (question 383, citing Matthew 25:41, 46 and Revelation 20:14-15).

Endless punishment. At the judgment Christ "will condemn" ungodly men and the devils "to be tormented without end", and the Augsburg Confession rejects those "who think that there will be an end to the punishments of condemned men and devils" (article 17).

The wicked, "who know not God, and obey not the Gospel of Jesus Christ", will be cast into eternal torments "and be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord", the Westminster Confession says, citing this passage (33.2).

The lost are not tormented forever. After the millennium the unrighteous dead are raised, and "fire from God will consume them and cleanse the earth", so that the universe is "freed of sin and sinners forever" (Fundamental Beliefs, 27).

Divided. Many evangelicals hold eternal conscious punishment, as the older Protestant confessions teach. A minority holds conditional immortality: "destruction" means the lost finally cease to exist, as Edward Fudge argued in The Fire That Consumes (1982), subtitled in later editions "The Biblical Case for Conditional Immortality".

title: Not Yet: What Must Come First
sum: Someone has told the believers that "the day of the Lord is already here", by a prophecy, a teaching or a letter claiming to be from Paul (2:1-2). The letter answers: that day cannot have come, because two things must happen first, "the rebellion" and the revealing of "the man of lawlessness, the son of ruin", who sets himself above every god and sits in the temple of God, claiming to be God (2:3-4). Paul had told them this when he was with them (2:5).

Something, and someone, is holding him back now, though "the mystery of lawlessness is at work already" (2:6-7). When he is revealed, with Satan's power and false signs, the Lord Jesus will destroy him with the breath of his mouth and the appearing of his coming (2:8-10). Those who refused to love the truth will believe the lie, and God sends them a working that leads them astray (2:10-12). The chapter then turns: God chose the readers for salvation, and they are to hold their ground and keep the traditions Paul taught them, by speech or by letter (2:13-15). A prayer closes it (2:16-17).
readings: Read as a future person at the end of history

The traditional reading, from Irenaeus and Chrysostom to modern futurists: the man of lawlessness is a single person, the Antichrist, who will appear just before Christ returns, and the temple is the Temple in Jerusalem (Irenaeus) or a temple rebuilt there (dispensationalists). The restrainer holds him back until God's time.
Read as a power in the church's history

The Protestant Reformers and their confessions took the man who sits "in the temple of God", the church, and claims God's place to be the papacy: Luther's Smalcald Articles cite 2:4, and the Westminster Confession of 1646 calls the pope "that man of sin and son of perdition". The Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. removed the identification from its Westminster text in 1903, while the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod's Brief Statement (1932) still says that the prophecies of 2:3-12 "have been fulfilled in the Pope of Rome and his dominion".

The readers knew of Antiochus IV, who set up an idol in the Temple (Daniel 11:31), and of the emperor Gaius, who in AD 40 ordered his statue set up in the temple of God. Preterist readers place the fulfillment in the crisis of the Jewish war and the Temple's fall in AD 70. Many critical scholars read the passage as apocalyptic language for an evil that the writer expected soon, without a precise historical figure in mind.

views.H: The crisis behind the chapter was practical: if the day of the Lord had begun, persecution might seem to prove it, and work and ordinary life might seem pointless (compare 3:6-12). The images came from history the readers knew: Antiochus IV and the "abomination that desolates" (Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:54), and Gaius Caligula's order of AD 40 to set up his statue "in the temple of God" (Josephus, Antiquities 18.261), never carried out. If the letter is Paul's, from about AD 51-52, the Temple still stood and that crisis was a recent memory.
views.C: This chapter is the center of the authorship debate. Critics argue that its timetable of signs (2:3-12) does not fit 1 Thessalonians 5:1-3, where the day comes suddenly, the way a thief comes at night; that 2:2 and 2:15 refer to a letter of Paul in a way that suits a later writer correcting how 1 Thessalonians was read; and that the passage has its own vocabulary ("the rebellion", "the one holding back", "appearing"). Defenders answer that Jewish apocalyptic writing often holds both together, sudden end and signs before it, as Jesus' own sayings do (Mark 13:5-37), and that a church claiming the day had already come needed exactly this answer. The text has several important variants ("man of sin", "from the beginning", "the Lord Jesus"): see the variant notes.
views.L: 2:1-12 is built like an apocalypse: a warning (2:1-2), a list of what must come first (2:3-4), a reminder (2:5), a hidden present (2:6-7), a revealing and a defeat (2:8), and a description of the deceiver and the deceived (2:9-12). The lawless one is shaped as a dark mirror of Christ: he has his own "revealing" (2:3, 6, 8), his own "coming" (2:9), his own signs and wonders and his own believers. The second half answers the first point by point: against those "on the road to ruin" who did not love the truth, God chose the readers "for salvation" by "faith in the truth" (2:13); against being shaken (2:2), they are to hold their ground (2:15).
views.J: The man of lawlessness is drawn from Daniel: the king who raises himself "above every god" (Daniel 11:36-37), the little horn who speaks against the Most High (Daniel 7:25), the abomination in the sanctuary (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11). Ezekiel's ruler of Tyre who says "I am a god! I sit in a seat for gods" (Ezekiel 28:2) lies behind "sit down in the temple of God". His defeat by "the breath of his mouth" is Isaiah 11:4, a messianic text. In their own setting these texts describe Antiochus IV and the arrogant empires, and God's victory over them. The chapter reads them, as Jesus did (Mark 13:14), as pointing beyond Antiochus to a final enemy.
views.T: No chapter has produced more speculation. The early church read it of a future Antichrist (Irenaeus, Chrysostom). Tertullian and Chrysostom took the restrainer to be the Roman Empire; Augustine listed the readings and confessed he did not know. The Reformers applied 2:4 to the papacy. Modern dispensational teachers make the restrainer the Holy Spirit and connect his removal with the rapture of the church. Catholic and Orthodox writers cite 2:15 for apostolic tradition alongside Scripture. The cards set out these answers.

deep.h: The man of lawlessness: four ways of reading
deep.b:
1. A future individual. The oldest reading. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.25) says the Antichrist will sit in the Temple in Jerusalem and links Paul with Daniel 8 and 9. Chrysostom thought Nero a "type" of him, a foretaste. The Catholic Catechism keeps the expectation of a final deception by "the Antichrist" without naming anyone (675), and dispensational teachers such as Thomas Ice expect the lawless one to be revealed after the church is taken away (see the card).

2. A power in church history. In the Reformation the figure who sits "in the temple of God", read as the church, was identified with the papacy. The Smalcald Articles (1537) call the pope "the very Antichrist" and cite 2:4; the Westminster Confession (1646) and the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) call him "that man of sin, and son of perdition". The Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. removed the line from its Westminster text in 1903, and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church kept that removal; American Lutheran bodies divided over whether the identification is doctrine or a "historical judgment" (see the card).

3. A first-century reference. Some read the passage against Caligula's attempt of AD 40 or against the Roman power that destroyed the Temple in AD 70. Preterist readers hold that it was fulfilled then.

4. A symbol of recurring evil. Idealist readers, and many critical scholars, take the man of lawlessness as the apocalyptic picture of evil reaching its full height, a pattern seen in many tyrants, before God's final victory. Augustine's own humility ("I frankly confess I do not know what he means", City of God 20.19) stands over all four.

deep.h: Signs first, or a thief in the night?
deep.b:
1 Thessalonians 5:2-3 says the day of the Lord comes the way a thief comes at night, suddenly, when people are talking of peace and safety. 2 Thessalonians 2:3 says it will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness. How do the two fit?

(1) Different audiences, one teaching. The thief comes suddenly on those who are not watching (1 Thessalonians 5:3-4); believers who know the signs are not taken by surprise. Jesus' sayings combine both: signs (Mark 13:5-23) and an unknown hour (Mark 13:32-37; Matthew 24:43). (2) Correction of a misreading. If some at Thessalonica took 1 Thessalonians to mean the day had already arrived, Paul (or a later writer) adds what must come first, to calm them. (3) Different authors. Many critical scholars see two views of the end that one writer would not hold in the same year, and take this as their strongest argument against Paul's authorship. The readers on this site can weigh the three.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the restrainer as the letter's way of saying 'not yet'
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with the published view that the restrainer is God or his plan. The letter's first aim in chapter 2 is pastoral: to stop panic (2:2) and to keep the church steady (2:15). The restrainer serves that aim whoever or whatever it is. Paul does not name it, because the readers already know (2:6); and for later readers the point that matters is not its identity but its function: evil is real and already at work (2:7), but it is held on a leash, and its time, "his own time" (2:6), is set by God. Read this way, the passage is less a puzzle to be solved than a way of saying "not yet, and not out of control". The many failed identifications in history, from Rome to the papacy, would then be a warning against using the passage to set dates, which is the very mistake the letter was written to correct.

echoes: Daniel 7:25; Daniel 8:11; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 11:36-37; Daniel 12:11; Ezekiel 28:2; Isaiah 11:4; Matthew 24:4-31; Mark 13:5-27; John 17:12; 1 John 2:18; Revelation 13; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:11; Deuteronomy 26:18; 1 Corinthians 11:2

settings.what: Teaching on the day of the Lord: what must come first
settings.by: Paul and his coworkers (the singular "I" breaks in at 2:5)
settings.to: the believers at Thessalonica, some of whom had been alarmed by a claim, said to come from Paul, that the day of the Lord was already here
settings.when: after a prophecy, teaching or letter had unsettled the church (2:2), and while persecution continued
settings.why: to stop panic and false teaching by reminding the readers of what Paul had told them in person: the day cannot have come, because the rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first, and his defeat by the Lord Jesus is certain. The aim is calm, not a timetable: the passage gives just enough to show that the claim is false. Knowing that the readers had already heard Paul's fuller teaching (2:5-6) explains why the passage is so allusive to us.
settings.readers: New converts who had been told the end had arrived would have heard: it has not; you have not missed it; evil has a set time and a set end.
views: Paul writes soon after 1 Thessalonians to correct a claim, perhaps drawn from a misreading of his first letter or from a prophecy, that the day had begun.
A later writer correcting end-time excitement
A follower of Paul, decades later, uses Paul's name to cool an end-time fervor in the churches. Trilling and Menken argue for a later writer.

settings.what: Thanksgiving for the readers' election, and a call to hold the traditions
settings.when: right after the description of those who are deceived
settings.why: to set the readers on the other side of the line just drawn: they are not among those who refused the truth, but were chosen by God, made holy by the Spirit and called through the good news. So they need not be shaken; they are to hold to what they were taught, by Paul's preaching and his letter. The "traditions" here are the apostles' teaching handed on to a church that had no New Testament yet.

settings.what: A prayer for comfort and strength
settings.when: as the close of the letter's central teaching
settings.why: to hand the frightened readers over to the Lord Jesus and the Father, who have already loved them and given them lasting comfort and hope, and to ask that they be made strong in what they do and say.

traditions.q: Who is the man of lawlessness who sits in the temple of God (2:3-4)? Has he been identified?
views: Before Christ returns the Church must pass through "a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers", and "the supreme religious deception is that of the Antichrist, a pseudo-messianism by which man glorifies himself in place of God and of his Messiah come in the flesh" (Catechism 675, citing 2:4-12). The Catechism names no one.

Following the fathers, a single deceiver at the end of history. John Chrysostom read "the lawless one" as the Antichrist who will come when Rome's power is removed, and saw Nero as a type, a foretaste, of him (Homily 4 on 2 Thessalonians); Irenaeus, honored in East and West, said he would sit in the Temple in Jerusalem (Against Heresies 5.25).

Historically, the papacy. The Smalcald Articles say "the Pope is the very Antichrist, who has exalted himself above and opposed himself against Christ", and cite 2:4 (part II, article 4). Lutheran churches in America later divided on how to hold it: the Missouri Synod's Brief Statement (1932) teaches that the prophecies of 2:3-12 "have been fulfilled in the Pope of Rome and his dominion" (43), while the American Lutheran Church's Sandusky Declaration (1938) accepted it as "the historical judgment of Luther" and left to God whether a "still more comprehensive fulfillment of 2 Thess. 2" may come, as the Wisconsin Synod's statement on the Antichrist records.

Historically, the papacy. The Westminster Confession of 1646 says the pope "is that Antichrist, that man of sin and son of perdition, that exalteth himself in the Church against Christ, and all that is called God" (25.6). The Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. rewrote 25.6 in 1903 and removed the identification, and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church's text keeps that removal.
The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) took over the same words: the pope "is that antichrist, that man of sin, and son of perdition" (26.4).

traditions.q: Will the church still be on earth when the lawless one is revealed (2:3-8), or will it be taken away first?
views: Taken away first. The one holding him back (2:7) is the Holy Spirit working through the church; when the church is raptured, "that ministry of the Holy Spirit will be removed as well", and only then can the lawless one be revealed, so the rapture comes before the tribulation (Thomas Ice). Some, Ice among them, also read "the rebellion" (2:3) as "the departure", the rapture itself.

Still on earth. "Before Christ's second coming the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers", which will unveil "the mystery of iniquity" (Catechism 675, citing 2:4-12). The Catechism does not say who or what holds the lawless one back.

Still on earth. The Missouri Synod's study of the end times says the "rapture" will occur "after the appearance and work of the Antichrist (2 Thess. 2:3)", and that the belief that the Holy Spirit and the church will be removed before the tribulation "has no Biblical support". On the restrainer it says: "We do not know what or whom he had in mind"; perhaps the Roman empire, but "one cannot be certain".

traditions.q: 'Hold the traditions you were taught, by speaking or by our letter' (2:15): is there apostolic tradition beside Scripture?
views: Yes. The Second Vatican Council cites this verse: the apostles warned the faithful "to hold fast to the traditions which they have learned either by word of mouth or by letter" (Dei Verbum 8). "Sacred tradition and Sacred Scripture form one sacred deposit of the word of God", and the Church does not draw its certainty "from Sacred Scripture alone"; the teaching office "is not above the word of God, but serves it" (Dei Verbum 9-10).

Yes: Scripture lives within Holy Tradition. Basil the Great wrote that of the church's teachings "some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us in a mystery by the tradition of the apostles" (On the Holy Spirit 27).

The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures are "the sole rule and standard" by which all teachers are judged; other writings, ancient or modern, are received only "as witnesses" to how the teaching was kept (Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm). What Paul taught by word is the same gospel now written.

No unwritten tradition binds the church. Nothing is to be added to Scripture "by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men", says the Westminster Confession (1.6), which cites 2:2 of this letter, the warning against false claims to speak for Paul, among its proofs.

Scripture is "the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience" (Second London Confession 1.1), and nothing is to be added to it by tradition (1.6). The traditions of 2:15 are the apostolic teaching now contained in the New Testament.

title: Work Quietly, Keep the Brother
sum: Paul asks for prayer for the spread of the message and for rescue from twisted and evil people, and assures the readers that the Lord is faithful (3:1-5). Then he turns to a problem he had already raised in 1 Thessalonians: some members are living "out of line", not working, living off others and meddling (3:6, 11).

He commands the church in the Lord's name to keep apart from them, reminds them that he and his partners worked night and day so as not to burden anyone (3:7-9), and repeats the rule he gave in person: "Whoever does not want to work should not eat either" (3:10). Those idle members are to work quietly and eat their own bread; anyone who refuses is to be marked and avoided, yet treated as a brother, not an enemy (3:12-15). The letter ends with a blessing of peace, a greeting in Paul's own hand, "the sign in every letter", and grace for all (3:16-18).
readings: Read as a word about work

Read on its own, 3:6-12 is one of the Bible's plainest statements of the dignity and duty of work, and has been quoted for that purpose as far afield as Lenin and the Soviet constitution of 1936. Careful readers note its limit: it speaks of those who are not willing to work, not of those who cannot.
Read in the light of chapter 2

Read with the rest of the letter, the idleness may be connected to the belief that the day of the Lord had come (2:2): why work if the world is ending? On this reading chapter 3 is the practical side of chapter 2's correction. R. Russell argued that the problem was social instead: poorer members living on the generosity of richer believers.
Read as a model of church discipline

3:14-15 gives a short and balanced pattern: name the problem, withdraw from the person, aim at shame that leads to change, and never treat him as an enemy. Churches with very different practices of discipline all appeal to it.

views.H: Most of the converts were probably manual workers and tradespeople. R. Russell (1988) argued that the problem was a social one: the poor of Greek and Roman cities depended on benefactors, and a church that shared its meals could be used in the same way. Paul and his partners refused support for this reason (3:8-9; 1 Thessalonians 2:9), working at their trade (Acts 18:3) so as to set an example. 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12 and 5:14 had already told the idle to work quietly; this chapter turns that advice into a command.
views.C: The parallels with 1 Thessalonians are close again: 3:8 nearly repeats 1 Thessalonians 2:9, and 3:16 and 3:18 echo 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and 5:28. Critics see a writer building from the earlier letter; defenders see the same writer returning to an unsolved problem. The greeting in Paul's own hand (3:17) is the second focus of the debate: is it Paul's real answer to a forged letter (2:2), or a later writer's way of making his letter look genuine? Both readings are argued by serious scholars.
views.L: The chapter is built of commands framed by blessings: a request and a blessing (3:1-5), the commands about the idle (3:6-15), a blessing (3:16), a signature (3:17) and a closing grace (3:18). The words for order and disorder repeat ("out of line" 3:6, 7, 11) and so do the words for work: "working night and day" (3:8), "does not want to work" (3:10), "doing no work at all but working hard at minding other people's business" (3:11), "work quietly" (3:12).
views.J: The rule of 3:10 has Jewish roots: the curse on Adam that he would eat bread by the sweat of his face (Genesis 3:19), the praise of work in Proverbs (6:6-11; 10:4); Paul himself, trained as a Pharisee, also worked with his hands (Acts 18:3; 20:34). The pattern of discipline, warning first and then withdrawal, matches the steps of Matthew 18:15-17, which build on the Torah's command to reprove a neighbor (Leviticus 19:17).
views.T: The chapter's saying on work was taken up in modern times by Lenin, who called it "the socialist principle". Its discipline passage is cited by churches with very different practices: Reformed and Baptist censures, and Anabaptist shunning; Catholic and Lutheran discipline follow the same steps of warning and exclusion. The card shows them side by side.

deep.h: Idle, or out of line? Two explanations
deep.b:
Why were some members not working? (1) End-time enthusiasm. If the day of the Lord had come (2:2), daily work could seem pointless. This links chapter 3 to chapter 2, and 1 Thessalonians mentions both the end (4:13-5:11) and quiet work (4:11-12) close together. (2) A social problem. R. Russell argued (1988) that a social explanation fits the evidence better than the end-time one: poor members may have depended on richer believers, living from their table and their gifts, as the urban poor depended on benefactors. Paul's insistence on his own example (3:7-9) and on eating "bread that is their own" (3:12) fits this. The two explanations can also be combined: the church's shared meals made idleness possible, and end-time excitement made it seem holy.

The word ataktos itself, "out of rank", allows both "idle" and "unruly". The meddling of 3:11 shows that idleness and disorder went together.

deep.h: 'Whoever does not want to work should not eat either': the life of a saying
deep.b: The saying is short enough to travel. It concerns members who are able to work and refuse, in a church that shared its food; it says nothing about the sick, the old or those who cannot find work, whom Paul elsewhere commands the church to help (Galatians 6:10; 1 Timothy 5:3-16). In later history it was quoted in many settings. Lenin, in The State and Revolution (1917), called "He who does not work shall not eat" "the socialist principle", and the 1936 Soviet constitution wrote it into article 12: "He who does not work, neither shall he eat." Readers have debated whether these uses keep the verse's limits: in the letter, it is a command to a church about its own members.

settings.what: A request for prayer, and confidence in the readers
settings.when: as the letter turns to its closing instructions; Paul is probably facing opposition where he is (Corinth, if he wrote soon after 1 Thessalonians; compare Acts 18:6, 12-17)
settings.why: to make the readers partners in the mission that had reached them, to remind them that their safety rests on the Lord's faithfulness, not on their own strength, and to prepare them, with an expression of confidence (3:4), for the command that follows.

settings.what: A command about members who live out of line and will not work
settings.by: Paul and his coworkers, speaking "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ"
settings.to: the whole church at Thessalonica, which must act ("hold yourselves apart", "mark that person out"), and, within it, the members who refused to work (3:12)
settings.when: after 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12 and 5:14 had already warned the idle, apparently without full success
settings.why: to restore order in a small community that shared meals and support. The rule binds members who are able to work and will not; it does not touch the sick or others who cannot (Paul's own phrase is "does not want to work"). It is given to a church about its own members. Its tools are example (3:7-9), command (3:12), and social distance aimed at shame and change (3:14), always within the family: the offender remains "a brother" (3:15). Knowing that the readers were poor converts living close together explains both the problem and the remedy.
settings.readers: The idle members heard a direct command to settle down and earn their bread; the rest heard that they were not to support idleness, but also not to drive the idle out as enemies.
views: The idle stopped working because they thought the day of the Lord had come (2:2).
The idle were poorer members living on richer believers, as the urban poor depended on benefactors; the shared meals made it easy (Russell).

settings.by: Paul, as the letter presents him, writing the last lines in his own hand
settings.to: all the believers at Thessalonica, the idle included ("all of you")
settings.when: at the end of the dictated letter, as in 1 Corinthians 16:21 and Galatians 6:11
settings.why: to wish them the peace the whole letter has aimed at, and to mark the letter as Paul's own, against any letter "that seems to be from us" (2:2): if Paul wrote it, by his own handwriting; if a follower wrote it, by claiming Paul's signature for it.
views: Paul adds his signature, as in his other letters, here stressing it because a false letter was circulating.
A follower writing in Paul's name stresses the signature to give his letter Paul's authority; the phrase "in every letter" fits a time when Paul's letters were already collected.

traditions.q: How should a church treat a member who will not obey (3:14-15)? Withdraw, shun, or exclude?
views: The head of a church is to correct by "pastoral charity, example of life, advice and exhortation", and only if these fail by penalties, applied "having in mind the restoration of justice, the reform of the offender, and the repair of scandal" (Code of Canon Law, canon 1311; compare 1341). The gravest, excommunication, is a "medicinal" penalty (canon 1312) that bars the person from the sacraments (canon 1331) and cannot be refused remission once the offender has given up his defiance (canon 1358).

The "lesser" ban excludes "manifest and obstinate sinners" from the Sacrament and the fellowship of the church "until they amend their lives", and ministers are not to mix "secular punishments with this ecclesiastical punishment" (Smalcald Articles, part III, article 9). The article does not cite this letter; it is the Lutheran form of the withdrawal 3:14 describes.

Church censures are "for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren"; the officers proceed "by admonition, suspension from the sacrament of the Lord's Supper for a season", "and by excommunication from the Church", according to the offense (Westminster Confession 30.3-4, citing 3:6, 14-15).

Members who are separated for a wicked life or false teaching are to be shunned "in eating, drinking, and other similar intercourse", so that they are shamed and brought to repent; yet the church "must not count them as enemies, but admonish them as brethren" and must help them in need (Dordrecht Confession, 1632, article 17, citing 3:14-15).

Each congregation has the power it needs for "order in worship and discipline" (Second London Confession 26.7, citing Matthew 18:17-18), and every member is "under the censures and government" of the local church "according to the rule of Christ" (26.12, citing 3:6, 14-15).
